clinicalPearls: Human herpesvirus 6 (chiefly HHV-6B) is acquired almost universally in early childhood and thereafter remains latent, capable of reactivation under immunosuppression
Primary infection in infants causes roseola infantum (exanthem subitum): several days of high fever followed by defervescence and a maculopapular rash as the child improves
It is a common cause of febrile seizures in young children owing to its neurotropism
In allograft recipients, especially after haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, reactivation causes post-transplant limbic encephalitis with amnesia, confusion, seizures, and hyponatraemia
MRI in HHV-6 encephalitis characteristically shows medial temporal lobe and limbic signal change, and CSF HHV-6 DNA PCR is usually positive
Chromosomally integrated HHV-6 (ciHHV-6), present in a minority of people, produces persistently very high viral DNA loads in every nucleated cell and can be mistaken for active infection
Antiviral agents active against HHV-6 (such as ganciclovir or foscarnet) are used for significant reactivation disease, particularly encephalitis in the immunocompromised
reference.pathophysiology: HHV-6 is a betaherpesvirus that infects and replicates in T lymphocytes and establishes lifelong latency in lymphocytes, monocytes, and the central nervous system. Primary infection in infancy produces a viraemic febrile illness; as the immune response develops the fever subsides and a rash may appear. The virus is neurotropic and can invade the limbic system, causing encephalitis when cellular immunity is impaired, as after stem-cell or solid-organ transplantation. Uniquely among human herpesviruses, HHV-6 can integrate its genome into host chromosomal telomeres; when this occurs in a germ cell the integrated virus is inherited in every somatic cell, producing extraordinarily high blood viral loads that do not indicate active replication and can confound diagnosis.
additionalDifferentials: Measles, rubella, and other viral exanthems of childhood
Other viral encephalitides including cytomegalovirus and enterovirus
Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), in which HHV-6 reactivation is often implicated
Bacterial meningitis or other causes of febrile seizures
additionalInvestigations: HHV-6 DNA PCR from cerebrospinal fluid in suspected encephalitis
Quantitative HHV-6 DNA PCR from plasma or whole blood to assess reactivation
MRI of the brain to demonstrate limbic and medial temporal involvement
Testing to identify chromosomally integrated HHV-6 (for example very high viral load in hair follicles or nails, or a consistent one-copy-per-cell ratio)
Serum sodium and full metabolic panel, as hyponatraemia accompanies limbic encephalitis
Electroencephalography where seizures or encephalopathy are present
redFlags: Amnesia, confusion, or seizures with limbic signal change after transplantation
Status epilepticus or prolonged febrile seizures
Rapidly declining conscious level suggesting encephalitis
Severe hyponatraemia accompanying suspected limbic encephalitis
reference.prognosis: Roseola in healthy children is benign and self-limiting; post-transplant HHV-6 limbic encephalitis is serious, with a risk of persistent memory impairment, epilepsy, or death, and outcome depends on prompt antiviral treatment and immune recovery.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the very high viral loads of chromosomally integrated HHV-6 as active infection and treating unnecessarily
Overlooking HHV-6 as a cause of encephalitis and amnesia in the early post-transplant period
Attributing all high fever with rash in infants to HHV-6 without considering other exanthems
Failing to link HHV-6 reactivation with DRESS and its relapsing course
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
UpToDate: Human herpesvirus 6 infection in adults and children
management: Treat serious disease such as post-transplant limbic encephalitis with ganciclovir or foscarnet, noting that aciclovir is not reliably effective against HHV-6
Manage roseola infantum in healthy children supportively with antipyretics and fluids, as it is self-limiting and needs no antiviral therapy
Provide supportive management of HHV-6-related febrile seizures and use antiepileptic therapy where encephalitic seizures occur
In transplant recipients, monitor blood viral load and reduce immunosuppression where feasible to aid immune recovery
Correct the hyponatraemia that accompanies limbic encephalitis and support neurological recovery
Identify chromosomally integrated HHV-6 to avoid misinterpreting persistently very high viral loads as active infection and overtreating
Escalate to specialist and critical care for encephalitis, refractory seizures or immunocompromised hosts
